Surah Ya-Sin

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Ya-Sin. From Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: "Its meaning is: O man (ya insan), in the dialect of Tayy." And from Ibn al-Hanafiyyah: "O Muhammad." And in a hadith: "Indeed Allah (Exalted is He) named me in the Qur'an with seven names: Muhammad, Ahmad, Ta-Ha, Ya-Sin, al-Muzzammil, al-Muddaththir, and ʿAbd Allah." It is also said: "O master (ya sayyid)." "Yis," with imalah (vowel inclination): ʿAli, Hamzah, Khalaf, Hammad, and Yahya.

The Qur'an is the Hakim — "by the Qur'an, the Wise" — an oath (qasam).

﴿By the Qur'an, the Wise﴾: meaning, possessing wisdom (dhi al-hikmah). Or, because it is a speaking proof of wisdom. Or, because it is a wise speech, and so it is described with the attribute of the one who speaks it.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 36, verse 3:

﴿Indeed, you are among the messengers﴾. This is the answer to the oath, and it is a rebuttal to the disbelievers when they said: "You are not a messenger."

"Upon a straight path" (﴿عَلَى صِرَاطٍ مُسْتَقِيمٍ﴾) is either a second predicate following another predicate, or a relative clause (ṣilah) modifying "the messengers" (al-mursalīn), meaning: those who were sent upon a straight path, that is, a straight way (ṭarīqah mustaqīmah), and this is Islam.

(p-96) ﴿Tanzīl﴾ (the revelation). With the lām in the accusative (naṣb), read by Ibn ʿĀmir (Shāmī) and the Kūfans except Abū Bakr, it is either governed by an implied verb, "Recite the revelation" (iqraʾ tanzīl), or it is a verbal noun (maṣdar), meaning "It was sent down as a sending down" (nuzzila tanzīl). The rest read it in the nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "It is the revelation" (huwa tanzīl), and the verbal noun here carries the sense of the passive participle (bi-maʿnā al-mafʿūl), meaning "that which has been sent down."

﴿al-ʿAzīz﴾ (the Mighty): the One who overcomes the minds of the obstinate (awhām dhawī al-ʿinād) through the eloquence (faṣāḥa) of the arrangement (naẓm) of His Book.

﴿al-Raḥīm﴾ (the Merciful): the One who draws the understandings (afhām) of those possessed of right guidance (ulī al-rashād) through the subtlety (laṭāfa) of the meaning of His address (khiṭāb).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 36, verse 6:

The lam in ﴿so that you may warn﴾ is connected to the meaning of "the messengers" (al-mursalin), i.e., "You have been sent so that you may warn a people

﴿whose fathers were not warned﴾." The "ma" (mā) is negative according to the majority (al-Jumhur), meaning: a people whose fathers had not been warned, based on His saying: ﴿so that you may warn a people to whom no warner had come before you﴾ [al-Sajdah: 3], and ﴿We did not send to them any warner before you﴾ [Saba': 44]. Or it is a relative pronoun (mawsulah) in the accusative as the second object, meaning: "the punishment" which their fathers were warned of, like His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have warned you of a near punishment﴾ [al-Naba': 40]. Or it is a verbal-masdar (masdariyyah), meaning: so that you may warn a people with the warning of their fathers, i.e., like the warning of their fathers.

﴿So they are heedless﴾. If you make "ma" negative, then it is connected to the negation, meaning: they were not warned, so they are heedless. Otherwise, it is connected to His saying: ﴿Indeed, you are among the messengers﴾ [Ya-Sin: 3] ﴿so that you may warn﴾, as you would say: "I sent you to so-and-so so that you may warn him, for he is heedless," or "so he is heedless."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 36, verse 7:

﴿Indeed, the Word has come into effect against most of them, so they do not believe﴾, meaning His saying: ﴿I will surely fill Hell with jinn and men all together﴾ [Hud: 119]. That is, this Word has attached itself to them, become firmly established against them, and become binding, because they are among those whom He knew would die in disbelief. Then He depicted their obstinacy in disbelief, and that there is no way for them to desist, by making them like those who are shackled and have their heads raised high, in that they do not turn toward the truth, nor bend their necks toward it, nor lower their heads for it; and like those who are confined between two barriers, unable to see what is in front of them or what is behind them, so that they have no reflection or insight, and that they are blind to looking at the signs of Allah, by His saying:

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 36, verse 8:

﴿Indeed, We have put yokes around their necks, and they reach to the chins, so they are held with their heads raised.﴾ Its meaning: the yokes reach up to the chins and are fastened against them.

﴿So they are with their heads raised (muqmahun)﴾: their heads are lifted up. It is said: "The camel qamaha (raised its head), so it is qamih," meaning when it has drunk its fill and raises its head. This is because the collar of the shackle that is on the neck of the one shackled sits at the junction of its two ends beneath the chin, a ring in which is the head of the pillar, extending out of the ring to the chin. So it does not let him lower his head, and he remains always with his head raised.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 36, verse 9:

﴿And We have placed before them a barrier, and behind them a barrier﴾, read with a fatha on the sin (سِينِ), [i.e., sadda, as opposed to ḍamm], by Hamza, ʿAlī and Ḥafṣ. It is said: what is the work of people is with the fatha, and what is the creation of Allah, such as a mountain and the like, is with the ḍamm.

﴿So We covered them﴾, i.e., We covered their sight, meaning We veiled it, and placed over it a covering.

﴿So they do not see﴾, the truth and the guidance. It is said: it was revealed concerning the Banu Makhzum, and that is because "Abu Jahl swore: 'If I see Muhammad praying, I will crush his head.' So he came to him while he was praying, and with him was a stone to strike him with it. When he raised his hand, it was bent back to his neck, and the stone stuck to his hand, until they freed it from it with difficulty. He returned to his people and informed them. Another Makhzumi said: 'I will kill him with this stone.' So he went, and Allah blinded his sight."

The Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 36, verse 10:

﴿It is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them; they will not believe.﴾ That is: whether warning them or leaving it is the same to them. The meaning is: whoever Allah has led astray in this manner, warning will not benefit him.

It is related that ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz (raḥimahu Allah) recited this verse to Ghaylan al-Qadari, and he said: "It is as if I had never recited it. I call you to witness that I repent of my statement about qadar." ʿUmar said: "O Allah, if he is truthful, then accept his repentance, and if he is lying, then set over him one who will show him no mercy." Then Hisham ibn ʿAbd al-Malik took him from his presence, cut off his hands and feet, and crucified him at the gate of Damascus.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 36, verse 11:

﴿Indeed, you can only warn one who follows the Reminder﴾ — i.e., only one who follows the Qur'an benefits from your warning,

﴿and fears the Most Merciful unseen﴾ — and fears the punishment of Allah, and has not seen Him,

﴿so give him good tidings of forgiveness﴾ — which is the pardoning of his sins,

﴿and a generous reward﴾ — i.e., Paradise.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 36, verse 12:

﴿Indeed, it is We who bring the dead to life﴾, for their resurrection after their death, or We bring them out of polytheism into faith,

﴿and We record what they have sent forward﴾, that is, the deeds they sent ahead of them, the righteous deeds and others, (p-98) ﴿and their traces﴾, that is, the good effects they left behind, such as a knowledge they taught, or a book they composed, or an endowment (habis), or a frontier fortification (ribat), or a mosque they built; or bad ones, such as an impost (wazifa) that some oppressors imposed. Likewise, every good custom or bad custom that is followed. Similar to this is His (Exalted) saying: ﴿Man will be informed on that Day of what he sent forward and left behind﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 13]: he sent forward of his deeds and left behind of his traces. It has also been said: they are their steps to the Friday prayer or to the congregational prayer.

﴿And every thing We have enumerated﴾, We have counted it and made it clear,

﴿in a manifest register (imam mubin)﴾, meaning the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), because it is the source of the books and the reference for them.

﴿And present to them the parable of the people of the town﴾. He gave them an example from their own speech: "I have of this kind (*ḍarb*) such-and-such," meaning "of this sort (*mithl*)," and "these things are of one kind (*ḍarb wāḥid*)," meaning of one pattern. The meaning is: "Present to them a parable like the parable of the people of the town," that is, Antioch. That is, relate to them a wondrous story, the story of the people of the town. The second example is an explanation of the first. The accusative of *idh* (when) is because it is a *badal* (substitute, in apposition) for "the people of the town."

﴿When the messengers came to them﴾: they were the messengers of Jesus, peace be upon him, sent to its people. He dispatched them as callers to the truth, and the people were worshippers of idols.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 36, verse 14:

﴿Idh﴾ is a substitute (badal) for the first "idh" (idh).

﴿We sent to them﴾, i.e., Jesus sent them by Our command,

﴿two﴾, truthful and very truthful. When they approached the city, they saw an old man tending his small flock, and he was Habib al-Najjar. He asked about their condition, and they said: "We are messengers of Jesus; we call you from the worship of idols to the worship of the Most Merciful." He said: "Do you have a sign?" They said: "We heal the sick, and we cure the blind and the leper." He had a son who had been ill for two years, so they wiped over him and he stood up, and Habib believed. The news spread, and a great many people were healed at their hands. The king summoned them and said to them: "Do we have a god other than our gods?" They said: "Yes. Who created you and your gods?" He said: "I will consider your matter." The people followed them and beat them. It was also said that they were imprisoned. Then Jesus sent Shamun (Simon), who entered disguised and mingled with the king's courtiers until they became familiar with him and reported his news to the king, who also grew fond of him. One day he said to him: "I have been told that you imprisoned two men. Have you heard their words?" He said: "No." So he summoned them. Shamun said: "Who sent you?" They said: "Allah, who created everything and provides for every living thing, and has no partner." He said: "Describe Him, and be brief." They said: "He does what He wills and decrees what He desires." He said: "And what is your sign?" They said: "What the king wishes." So a blind boy was brought, and they prayed to Allah, and the boy regained his sight. Shamun said: "Do you see? If you asked your god to do the like of this, it would be for you and for him the honour?" The king said: "I have no secret from you. Our god does not hear, does not see, does not harm, and does not benefit." Then he said: "If your god can raise the dead, we will believe in him." So they called a boy who had died seven days earlier, and he stood up and said: "I was put into seven valleys of fire because of the polytheism I died upon, and I warn you of what you are in." They believed. He said: "The gates of heaven were opened, and I saw a youth of beautiful face interceding for these three." The king said: "And who are they?" He said: "Shamun and these two." The king was amazed, and when Shamun saw that his words had affected him, he advised him, and he believed, and a people believed, and whoever did not believe, Gabriel shouted at them and they perished.

﴿But they denied them﴾, i.e., the people of the city denied the two messengers,

﴿so We strengthened﴾, i.e., We reinforced them. "Fa-azzaznā" is read by Abu Bakr from "azzahu, yuʿizzuhu" (he overpowered him), meaning: so We overpowered and subdued,

﴿with a third﴾, who was Shamun. The object is omitted because the intended point is the one by whom strength was given, namely Shamun, and the subtle arrangement he made, until the truth prevailed and falsehood was humbled. When speech is directed toward one of the aims, its context and orientation are made toward that aim, as if what is other than it were discarded.

﴿They said: "Indeed we are sent to you"﴾, i.e., the three said to the people of the city.

《They said》 — that is, the people of the town.

"They said: You are only mortals like us." The word "بَشَرٌ" (basharun, "mortals/human beings") is in the nominative here, but in the aya "﴿ما هَذا بَشَرًا﴾" [Yusuf: 31] it is in the accusative, because the negation with "إلّا" (illa, "except/only") has annulled the negation of "ما" (ma), so "ما" no longer retains any resemblance to "لَيْسَ" (laysa, "is not"), which is the one that governs by its own action (i.e., the one that is positive in effect).

"And the Most Merciful has not sent down anything" — that is, revelation.

"You are only liars" — meaning: you are nothing but liars.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 36, verse 16:

﴿They said, "Our Lord knows that we are indeed sent to you."﴾ He emphasized the second clause with the particle lam (*lam*, emphatic lam), but not the first, because the first is the opening of a statement, while the second is a response to a denial. So it requires additional emphasis. And "our Lord knows" (*rabbuna ya'lamu*) functions in the sense of an oath for emphasis. Likewise is their saying, "God bears witness" (*shahida Allah*) and "God knows" (*alima Allah*). (p-١٠٠)
And Our duty is only to convey the clear message. That is: the plain, manifest conveying, made evident by the signs that testify to its truth.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 36, verse 18:

﴿They said: Indeed we take omen from you.﴾ That is, we consider you an ill omen (tashaammana bikum). This is because they disliked their religion and their souls recoiled from it. It is the habit of the ignorant to regard as auspicious everything toward which they incline and which their natures accept, and to regard as inauspicious everything from which they recoil and which they dislike. So if affliction or blessing befell them, they would say: "It is due to the ill omen of this one" or "due to the blessing of that one." It is also said that the rain was withheld from them, and so they said this.

﴿Unless you desist﴾, from this speech of yours,

﴿we will surely stone you﴾, we will kill you, or we will expel you, or we will revile you,

﴿and a painful punishment will surely touch you from us﴾, that is, the punishment of the Fire will befall you, and it is the most severe punishment.

﴿They said, "Your omen is with you."﴾ That is, the cause of your ill omen,

﴿with you﴾, which is disbelief.

﴿Is it that﴾, with the interrogative hamza (hamzat al-istifham) and the conditional particle (harf al-shart), "Kufan and Shami",

﴿you were reminded﴾, that is, admonished and invited to Islam. The apodosis of the conditional (jawab al-shart) is elided, and its estimated form is "you would be superstitious" (taṭayyartum). "Ayin", with a long hamza followed by a kasra-vowelled ya, "Abu 'Amr", and "Ayin", with a short hamza followed by a kasra-vowelled ya, "Makki and Nafi'". "Dhukkirtum", with the lightened form, "Yazid".

﴿Rather, you are a people who exceed the bounds﴾, transgressing the limit in disobedience. Therefore the ill omen came upon you from your own side, not from the side of God's messengers and their admonition. Or, "Rather, you are excessive in your error and your deviation, in that you consider ill omen from those with whom one must seek blessing, namely the messengers of God."

The Qur'anic quotations are rendered in English in the ﴿ ﴾ markers as instructed.

﴿And there came from the farthest part of the city a man running.﴾ He was Habib al-Najjar (the carpenter), and he was in a cave in the mountain, worshipping Allah. When news of the messengers reached him, he came to them and openly declared his religion, and said: "Do you ask of those who sent you any wage?" They said: "No."

﴿He said: "O my people, follow the messengers.﴾

Follow those who do not ask you for any wage (for conveying the message),

and who are themselves rightly guided. That is, the messengers. Then they said: "Are you upon the religion of these people?!" And he said:

﴿And what is the matter with me that I should not worship He who originated me﴾, created me,

﴿and to Him you will be returned﴾, and to Him is your return. "وَما لِي" (wa mā lī), "حَمْزَةُ" (Ḥamzah).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 36, verse 23:

(p-101) ﴿Shall I take﴾ — with two hamzas, according to Kufan reading (al-Kufi, i.e., the reading transmitted by ʿĀṣim, Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī and others of Kufa) —

﴿gods besides Him﴾, meaning the idols,

﴿if the Most Merciful wills harm for me﴾: this is a conditional clause (sharṭ, a grammatical condition), whose response (jawāb) is: ﴿their intercession will avail me nothing, nor can they save me﴾, from something disliked; and "nor can they save me" (wa-lā yunqidhūni), and "hear me" (fa-isma'ūni), in both states, is the reading of Yaʿqūb.

﴿Indeed, then I would be﴾ that is: if I were to take (them as gods),

﴿surely in clear error﴾, manifest and evident. When he advised his people, they began to stone him, so he hastened toward the messengers before he could be killed, and said to them:
﴿Indeed, I have believed in your Lord, so listen to me.﴾ That is: listen to my faith, so that you may bear witness for me to it. And when he was killed,

﴿It was said﴾ to him, ﴿"Enter Paradise."﴾ His grave is in the market of Antioch (Antakiya). He did not say "it was said to him" (qīla lahu), because the speech is presented to explain what was said, not to explain the one addressed, even though he was known. In this there is an indication that Paradise is created. Al-Ḥasan said: When the people intended to kill him, God raised him to Himself, and he is in Paradise, and he will not die until the heavens and the earth perish. So when he entered Paradise and saw its bliss,

﴿He said, "Would that my people knew."﴾
"With what my Lord has forgiven me," meaning: by the forgiveness of my Lord to me, or by that which He forgave me. "And made me of the honored ones," (by admitting me to) Paradise.

"And We did not send down upon his people, after him, any host from the heaven, nor were We ever going to send down [any host]."

**Commentary:**

﴿وَما أنْـزَلْنا﴾ — "ما" is negating (i.e., it is a negative particle).

﴿عَلى قَوْمِهِ﴾ — [upon] his people, the people of Habib.

﴿مِن بَعْدِهِ﴾ — that is, after his killing, or after his being raised up (taken up to heaven).

﴿مِن جُنْدٍ مِنَ السَماءِ﴾ — [any] host from the heaven, to punish them.

﴿وَما كُنّا مُنْـزِلِينَ﴾ — It was not fitting in Our wisdom that We should send down, for the destruction of the people of Habib, a host from the heaven. This is because Allah (Exalted) decreed the destruction of every people in certain ways and not others, for a wisdom that required this.

﴿In kānat﴾ (it was not), i.e. the seizing (al-akhdhah), or the punishment (al-ʿuqūbah),

﴿illā ṣayḥatan wāḥidah﴾ (except one cry): Jibrīl (peace be upon him) cried out one cry,

﴿fa-idhā hum khāmidūn﴾ (then they are extinguished), i.e. dead, just as fire is extinguished. (p-102) The meaning is that God sufficed for their affair with the cry of one angel, and did not send down for their destruction any of the hosts of heaven, as He did on the day of Badr and the day of al-Khandaq (the Trench).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 36, verse 30:

﴿Alas for the servants! No messenger comes to them but they mock him.﴾ Al-hasrah (regret): intense remorse. This is a call (nida') to regret concerning them, as if it were said to it: "Come, O regret, for this is one of the states in which you ought to be present, namely the state of their mocking of the messengers." The meaning is that they deserve that those who feel regret should feel regret over them, and that those who lament should lament over their condition, or that they are the object of regret from the angels and the believers among the two groups (jinn and humankind).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 36, verse 31:

﴿Did they not see﴾: did they not know (ألَمْ يَعْلَمُوا)?

﴿How many generations We destroyed before them﴾: "كَمْ" (kam, "how many") is in the accusative, governed by "أهْلَكْنا" (ahlaknā, "We destroyed"). "يَرَوْا" (yarawā, "they see") is suspended from acting on "كَمْ" (kam), because "كَمْ" is not governed by any operator preceding it. It is used either interrogatively or declaratively, since its original function is interrogative, but its meaning takes effect within the clause. His saying: ﴿that they, to them, do not return﴾ is a substitute (badal) for "كَمْ أهْلَكْنا" (kam ahlaknā), in meaning and not in wording. Its sense is: "Did they not see the abundance of Our destruction of the generations before them, that they do not return to them?"

Note: The Arabic terms used here are transliterated with glosses as follows: *ta'līq* (suspension of the verb's governing effect), *badal* (substitute/apposition), and *i'rāb* (grammatical case-analysis) where relevant.

"﴿And indeed, all of them, they will all be gathered before Us, brought forward.﴾" — "لَمّا" (lammā), with the doubled mīm, is read by Ibn ʿĀmir (Shāmī), ʿĀṣim and Ḥamzah, in the sense of "illā" (except/only), and "in" is negating; the rest read it with the mīm lightened, taking "mā" as a particle of emphasis (ṣilah lil-taʾkīd), and "in" as the lightened form of the heavy (muthaqqalah) "inna," which is inevitably followed by the lām. The tanwīn on "kullun" is a substitute (ʿiwaḍ) for the genitive noun that was omitted. The meaning: "Indeed all of them are gathered, brought together, and brought forward for reckoning, or for punishment." He described "kullun" by "jamīʿun" because "kullun" conveys totality, and "jamīʿun" is on the pattern faʿīl in the sense of maf ʿūl; its meaning is being brought together, i.e., the place of assembly gathers them.

﴿وَآيَةٌ لَهُمُ﴾ [And a sign for them] is a subject (mubtada') or a predicate (khabar), meaning: "And a sign and an indication that God resurrects the dead is the giving of life to the dead earth." It is also permissible for "āyah" to be in the nominative as a subject (mubtada'), with "lahum" as its qualifying descriptor (sifah), and its predicate is: ﴿الأرْضُ المَيْتَةُ﴾ [the dead earth], meaning the dry earth. The word "al-mayyitah" is read with a shaddah (tashdid) by Madani [the reading of the people of Madina].

﴿أحْيَيْناها﴾ [We gave it life], with the rain. This is a resumptive explanatory clause (isti'naf bayan) clarifying why the dead earth is a sign. Likewise, "naslakh" [We strip away]. It is also permissible to describe "al-ard" [the earth] and "al-layl" [the night] by a verb, because by them is meant general, unrestricted categories, not a specific earth or night. So they are treated like indefinite nouns (nakirat) in being described by verbs. A similar usage is the line of poetry:

"And indeed I pass by the base man who abuses me..."

﴿وَأخْرَجْنا مِنها حَبًّا﴾ [And We brought forth from it grain], where the word refers to the genus (jins).

﴿فَمِنهُ يَأْكُلُونَ﴾ [and from it they eat]. He placed the adverbial phrase (zarf) first to show that grain is the thing on which most of livelihood depends, and by which the welfare of people is sustained through their sustenance from it. When it becomes scarce, famine comes, harm befalls, and then destruction is present and affliction descends.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 36, verse 34:

﴿And We placed in it﴾, in the earth,

﴿gardens﴾, orchards,

﴿of date-palms and grapevines, and We caused springs to gush forth in it﴾, "min" (from), is superfluous (zā'idah), according to al-Akhfash; according to others, the object is omitted, its estimated sense being: "that from which they benefit."

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 36, verse 35:**

﴿That they may eat of its fruit﴾. The pronoun refers to God (exalted is He), meaning: that they may eat of what God created of the fruit. "مِن ثُمُرِهِ" (*min thumurihi*, "of its fruit"), read by Hamzah and Ali.

﴿And what their hands made﴾. That is, and of what their hands made, of planting, watering, pollination, and other works, until the fruit reaches its completion. The meaning is that the fruit itself is the act and creation of God, and it contains traces of the toil of the children of Adam. The original form was "مِن ثَمَرِنا" (*min thamarina*, "of Our fruit"), as in "وَجَعَلْنا" ("and We made") and "وَفَجَّرْنا" ("and We caused to gush"), so the speech shifted from the first person to the third person by way of *iltifat* (a shift in grammatical person, a technique of address). It is also permissible for the pronoun to refer to the palm trees, with the vines left unmentioned, since it is known that they share the ruling of the palm trees, as the eating of their fruit is linked to them. It is also permissible that it means "مِن ثَمَرِ المَذْكُورِ" (*min thamari al-madhkur*, "of the fruit of what has been mentioned"), that is, the gardens, as Ru'bah said:

*"In it are streaks of white and speckled patches,*
*as if on the skin were the spreading of leprosy."*

When he was asked about this, he said: "I meant: 'as if that (was)'."

"وَما عَمِلَتْ" (*wa ma 'amilat*, "and what she made"), read by the Kufan reciters other than Hafs. It is written that way in the Qur'an copies of the people of Kufa, while in the copies of the people of the two Holy Cities, Basra, and Syria it is written with the pronoun. It is also said that "ما" is negative, meaning that the fruit is God's creation and no human hands made it, nor are people able to do so.

﴿Will they not then be grateful?﴾ This is a rebuke for delay and an exhortation to give thanks for the blessing.

Glory be to Him who created the pairs, the kinds, all of them, from what the earth grows, from the date palms, the trees, the crops and the fruits, and from themselves, the offspring, males and females, and from what they do not know: and of pairs which Allah has not revealed to them, and which they have not been able to attain knowledge of. So in the valleys and the seas there are things that people do not know.

﴿And a sign for them is the night: We strip from it the day﴾, we bring the day out of it with a bringing-out, such that nothing of the light of day remains with it. Or we draw off the light from it as one draws off a white shirt, so that the very time is laid bare, like a black Zanji figure, because the original state of what lies between the heaven and the earth, of air, is darkness. So part of it is clothed with the light of the sun, like a dark house in which a lamp has been lit. When the lamp is extinguished, it becomes dark.

﴿Then behold, they are in darkness﴾, entering into the dark.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 36, verse 38:**

﴿And the sun runs﴾, and a sign for them is that the sun runs,

﴿to a resting place for it﴾, to a limit set for it, appointed and determined, which it reaches from its orbit (falak) at the end of the year. It is likened to the resting place of a traveller when he has completed his journey. Or: "to a limit for it from its course each day, in the sight of our eyes," which is the setting point (al-Maghrib). Or: to the end of its affair at the cessation of the world.

﴿That﴾, the running upon that determined measure and precise calculation,

﴿is the decree of the Almighty﴾, the Victorious through His power over everything that can be decreed,

﴿the All-Knowing﴾, of everything that can be known.

﴿And the moon﴾ is in the accusative, governed by a verb that is explained by the following ﴿We have determined it﴾. It is also read in the nominative by Makki, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Sahl, on the basis of the inchoative (ibtida', a nominal sentence beginning with its subject). In that case the predicate is "We have determined it," or it is governed by "and a sign for them is the moon."

﴿Stations﴾: there are twenty-eight stations. The moon does not descend into one of them each night without passing beyond it or falling short of it, according to a uniform measure. It travels through them from the night of the new moon to the twenty-eighth night, then it is hidden for two nights, or one night, when the month has only twenty-nine days. In "We have determined it stations," there must be an implied noun before "stations," because it makes no sense to say that the moon itself is determined as stations. The meaning is either "We have determined its light, so that it increases and decreases," or "We have determined its course as stations," in which case "stations" is an adverb of time or place (zarf). When it reaches the last of its stations, it becomes thin and curved.

﴿Until it returns like the old date stalk﴾: this is the stalk of the bunch of dates when it dries out (p-105) and bends. Its morphological pattern is fu'lun, from al-in'iraj, which means bending.

﴿Ancient﴾: the aged, withered one. When it becomes old, it becomes thin, bent and yellow. Thus the moon is compared to it in three respects.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 36, verse 40:

﴿Nor is it for the sun to overtake the moon﴾, i.e., it is not made easy for it, nor is it fitting or proper for it,

﴿to overtake the moon﴾, so that it would meet with it at one time and encroach upon its dominion, thereby extinguishing its light, because each of the two luminaries has a dominion of its own: the dominion of the sun is by day, and the dominion of the moon is by night,

﴿nor does the night outstrip the day﴾, i.e., the night does not precede the day. That is, the sign of the night does not outstrip the sign of the day, and these are the two luminaries. The matter continues in this arrangement until the Resurrection, when Allah will join the sun and the moon together, and the sun will rise from its west.

﴿And each﴾, the tanwin here is a substitute for the genitive noun that was omitted, i.e., "and all of them," and the pronoun refers to the suns and the moons,

﴿in an orbit they swim﴾, they travel.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 36, verse 41:

﴿And a sign for them is that We carried their offspring﴾, "dhurriyyatahum" (their offspring), "Madani and Shami" (read by the Medinan and Syrian readers),

﴿in the laden ship﴾, i.e., the filled (al-mamlu'). By "dhurriyyah" (offspring) is meant the children, and those whose carrying concerns them. They used to send them off to trade by land or by sea. Or it means the fathers, because the word is among the terms with opposite meanings (addad). "Al-fulk" (the ship), according to this view, is the ship of Nuh (peace be upon him). It was also said that the meaning of God carrying their offspring in it is that He carried their forefathers in it, while their loins held them and their offspring. He mentioned "their offspring" rather than "them" because it is more emphatic in bestowing favour upon them.
"And We have created for them of the like of it [that] they ride" — of the like of the ship (al-fulk), [namely] of the camels, which are the ships of the land.

ﷺ-free passage, short. Translate faithfully, keeping Qur'anic quotations in ﴿ ﴾ with plain meaning inside.

﴿And if We will, We drown them﴾ in the sea,

﴿then there is no one to answer their cry for help﴾, meaning, no one to rescue them; or: no rescue,

﴿nor are they saved﴾, meaning, they are not delivered.

Except as a mercy from Us and an enjoyment (of life) until a time appointed. ﴿Except as a mercy from Us and an enjoyment until a time appointed.﴾ That is: "They will not be rescued except out of mercy from Us, and for the enjoyment of life until the end of the appointed term." So both (words), ﴿raḥmatan﴾ and ﴿matā'an﴾, are in the accusative as an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu, the accusative of purpose/cause).

﴿And when it is said to them, "Fear what is before you and what is behind you"﴾, i.e., what has preceded of your sins and what has come after, of what you are doing, from now on; or: like the calamities with which the nations that denied their prophets were afflicted; and what is behind you of the matter of the Hour, or the trial of this world and the punishment of the Hereafter.

﴿So that you may be shown mercy﴾, so that you may be upon the hope of Allah's mercy. The jawab (apodosis, the main clause answering the conditional) of إذا (idhā, "when") is implied, i.e., "they turn away." Its omission is permissible because his saying:

...indicates it. The first "min" (مِن) is for emphasizing the negation, and the second is partitive (*lil-tab'id*, "some of"). That is, their habit (*da'b*) is to turn away at every sign and admonition.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 36, verse 47:**

﴿And when it is said to them﴾, to the polytheists of Makkah,

﴿"Spend from what Allah has provided you"﴾, i.e., give charity to the poor,

﴿those who disbelieved say to those who believed, "Shall we feed one whom, if Allah willed, He would feed?"﴾. From Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father): There were *zanadiqa* (heretics, freethinkers) in Makkah, and when they were commanded to give charity to the needy, they said, "No, by Allah! Will Allah make him poor and we feed him?!" ﴿"You are only in manifest error"﴾. This is either the words of Allah to them, or the quoted words of the believers to them, or it is part of their reply to the believers.

And they say, "When is this promise, if you are truthful?"

That is, the promise of resurrection and the Last Day.

﴿If you are truthful﴾ in what you say. This is an address to the Prophet (ﷺ) and his companions.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 36, verse 49:

﴿ما يَنْظُرُونَ﴾: yantaẓirūn (they await), i.e., they are waiting.

﴿إلا صَيْحَةً واحِدَةً﴾: this is the first blast (al-nafkhah al-ūlā) of the Trumpet.

﴿تَأْخُذُهم وهم يَخِصِّمُونَ﴾: Ḥamzah read yakhaṣṣimūn with the khā' vowelless and the ṣād lightened, from khaṣamahu (to defeat him in a dispute) when one overcomes him in argument. The rest read the ṣād with a shadda, i.e., yakhiṣṣimūn, with the tā' assimilated into the ṣād. However, with a fatḥa on the khā', Makkī read it by transferring the vowel of the assimilated tā' onto it; with a sukūn on the khā', Madanī read it; and with a kasra on the yā' and the khā', Yaḥyā read it, making the yā' follow the khā' in kasra. Others read it with a fatḥa on the yā' and a kasra on the khā'.

The meaning: "It will seize them while some of them are disputing with others in their dealings."

ﷺ not needed here. Translation:

(p-107) ﴿So they will not be able to make a bequest﴾: meaning, they will not be able to convey any instruction (tawsiyah) regarding any of their affairs.

﴿Nor will they return to their families﴾: meaning, they will not be able to return to their dwellings; rather, they will die right where they are when they hear the Blast (al-Sayhah).

"And the Trumpet will be blown, [and] that is the second blast. "Al-Sur" (the Trumpet) is the horn, or it is the plural of "sūrah" (form).

﴿Then, behold, they will rise from the graves﴾, i.e., the graves,

﴿to their Lord they will hasten﴾, they will go forth quickly. The verb yansilūn may be read with a kasra or a damma on the sīn.

"They will say: "Woe to us! Who has raised us up from our resting-place?"" 

Note: the translation below follows the Arabic text as given.

﴿They say﴾, i.e., the disbelievers,

﴿"Woe to us! Who has raised us from our resting-place?"﴾ i.e., who has resurrected us (anshara-na) from our sleeping place (madja'-ina). The pause here is a obligatory pause (waqf lazim), according to Hafs and Mujahid. For the disbelievers there is a brief slumber in which they find the taste of sleep; then, when the people of the graves are called, they say, "Who has raised us?" ﴿"This is what the Most Merciful promised, and the messengers spoke the truth."﴾ This is the speech of the angels, or of the God-fearing, or of the disbelievers, who recall what they heard from the messengers and answer themselves with it, or some of them answer others. The "ma" (in ﴿ma wa'ada﴾) is a verbal-source particle (masdariyya), and its meaning is: "This is the promise of the Most Merciful and the truthfulness of the messengers," by naming the promised thing and the thing confirmed as "the promise" and "the truthfulness." Or it is a relative particle (mawsula), and its implied sense is: "This is that which the Most Merciful promised and that which the messengers spoke truly," i.e., that concerning which the messengers spoke truly.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 36, verse 53:

﴿It will be but one shout﴾, namely the final blast (al-nafkhah al-akhirah),

﴿and behold, they will all be brought before Us﴾, for the reckoning. Then he mentioned what will be said to them on that Day:

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 36, verse 55:

﴿Indeed, the companions of the Garden today﴾, read with two ḍammas (the short vowel *u*) according to al-Kūfiyy (the Kufan reader) and al-Shāmiyy (the Syrian reader), and with one ḍamma and a sukūn (absence of vowel) according to al-Makkiyy (the Meccan reader), Nāfiʿ, and Abū ʿAmr. The meaning is: "in what occupation?" And [it is] an occupation that cannot be described, namely the deflowering of virgins, on the banks of rivers, under the trees, or the striking of lutes, or the hospitality of al-Jabbār (the Almighty).

﴿Fākihūn (enjoying)﴾ is the second predicate (khabar thānī). It is read as "fakihūn" by Yazīd, and "al-fākih" and "al-fakih" mean: one who lives in luxury, who takes pleasure. From this comes "al-fākihah" (fruit), because it is something one takes pleasure in. Likewise "al-fukāhah" (merriment).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 36, verse 56:

﴿هُمْ﴾, a mubtada' (subject of a nominal sentence),

﴿وَأزْواجُهُمْ﴾, a conjunction (ʿatf) upon it,

﴿فِي ظِلالٍ﴾, a ḥāl (circumstantial qualifier). It is the plural of "ẓill," which is the place that the sun does not reach, like "dhi'b" and "dhi'āb" (wolf and wolves). Or it is the plural of "ẓullah," like "burmah" and "biram" (cooking pot and pots). Its evidence is the recitation of Ḥamzah and ʿAlī: "ẓulalin," the plural of "ẓullah," which is that which shades one from the sun.

﴿عَلى الأرائِكِ﴾, the plural of "al-arīkah," which is a couch within a canopied bower (ḥajalah), or the bedding within it.

﴿مُتَّكِئُونَ﴾, a khabar (predicate). Or "fī ẓilālin" is the khabar, and "ʿalā al-arā'ik" is a resumed (mustaʾnaf) sentence.

For them therein is fruit, and for them is whatever they call for (yaddaʿūna).

"Yadda'ūna" is of the form "yaftaʿilūna," from "al-duʿāʾ" (supplication, calling for). That is: whatever the people of Paradise call for comes to them. Or it means "they wish for," from their saying: "ud'u ʿalayya mā shi'ta" (call down upon me whatever you wish), meaning: "tamannahu ʿalayya" (wish it for me). This is related by al-Farrāʾ. It may also derive from "al-daʿwā" (claim), meaning they do not claim what they do not deserve.

﴿Salamun﴾ is a substitute (*badal*, a grammatical term meaning "substitute" or "apposition") for "*mā yadda'ūn*" (what they ask for). It is as if He said to them: "Peace is said to them" ﴿qawlan min Rabbin Raḥīm﴾ (a word from a Lord, Most Merciful). The meaning is that Allah greets them with peace, through the angels or without an intermediary, as an honouring of them. That is what they wish for, and they have it; they are not prevented from it. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: "The angels enter upon them with greeting from the Lord of the worlds."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 36, verse 59:

﴿Wamtazu al-yawma ayyuhā al-mujrimūn﴾ ("And separate yourselves today, O guilty ones"), i.e., withdraw from the believers and stand apart, and be set apart on your own. That will be when the believers are gathered and led to Paradise. According to al-Ḍiḥāk: "For every disbeliever there is a house of Fire, in which he will be; he will neither see nor be seen, forever." And he (Ḍiḥāk) says that they will be told on the Day of Resurrection:

Qur'anic quotation: "Did I not charge you, O children of Adam, that you should not worship Satan? Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy."

Al-'ahd (covenant, charge): the command or instruction. "'Ahida ilayhi" means he charged him, when he enjoined him.

The covenant of Allah with them: what He placed within them of the proofs of reason (adillat al-'aql), and what He sent down to them of the proofs of revelation (dala'il al-sam').

Worshipping Satan (ibadat al-shaytan): obeying him in what he whispers to them (yuwaswisu bihi ilayhim) and what he makes attractive to them (yuzayyinuhu lahum).

﴿And that you worship Me﴾: monotheize Me, and obey Me.

﴿This﴾: a reference to what was enjoined upon them, namely disobedience to Satan and obedience to the Most Merciful,

﴿is a straight path﴾: that is, a path that is eloquent in its straightness, and there is no path more upright than it.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 36, verse 62:**

﴿And he had already led astray from among you a great throng﴾: read as جِبِلا (*jibilan*), with a kasra on the jim and the ba' and with tashdid (doubling of the ba'), by Madani, ʿĀṣim and Sahl; as جُبُلًّا (*jubullan*), with a damma on the jim and the ba' and with tashdid, by Yaʿqub; as جُبْلًا (*jublan*), unstressed (mukhaffafan), by Shami and Abu ʿAmr; and as جُبُلًا (*jubulan*), with a damma on the jim and the ba' and the lam lightened (taḥfīf al-lām), by the rest of the readers. These are dialectal variant forms (lughāt, "dialects" or "variant pronunciations") with the same meaning, "creation."

﴿...many. Did you not then use your reason?﴾: an interrogative of rebuke (istifhām taqrīʿ, a question used to reproach) for their failure to benefit from reason.
﴿This is Hell, which you were promised.﴾ (It is said to them) "with it" — that is, the statement is directed at them with it.
"Burn in it today for what you used to disbelieve." [Qur'an 36:64]. "Enter it" (udkhulūhā), because of your disbelief and your denial of it.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 36, verse 65:

﴿Today We shall seal their mouths﴾, i.e., We shall prevent them from speaking,

﴿and their hands will speak to Us, and their feet will bear witness to what they used to earn﴾. It is related that they would deny and dispute, so their neighbors, their families, and their clans would bear witness against them, and they would swear: "We were not polytheists." Then their mouths would be sealed, and their hands and feet would speak.

In a hadith: "On the Day of Resurrection the servant will say: 'Indeed, I do not permit against myself except a witness from myself.' Then his mouth will be sealed, and his limbs will be told: 'Speak!' and they will speak of his deeds. Then he will be left free between himself and speech, and he will say: 'Away with you, and destruction! It was on your behalf that I was contending.'"

And if We willed, We would have obliterated their eyes, meaning We would have blinded them and taken away their sight. *Al-ṭamsu* (الطَّمْس, obliteration) means effacing the slit of the eye until it becomes smooth, as if it had been wiped over.

﴿So they would race to the path﴾, with the preposition omitted so that the verb reaches its object directly. The original is فاسْتَبَقُوا إلى الصِراطِ, "they raced to the path."

﴿Then how would they see?﴾ (p-١١٠) How would they see then, when We have obliterated their eyes?!

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 36, verse 67:

﴿And had We willed, We would have transformed them﴾ [out of] their places, [turning them into] monkeys, or swine, or stones.

﴿In their places﴾: "ʿalā makānātihim" (in the plural form) is the reading of Abu Bakr and Hammad, and al-Makānah and al-Makān are one and the same, like al-Muqāmah and al-Muqām. That is: We would have transformed them in their dwellings, where they commit their sins.

﴿So they would not have been able to proceed﴾, meaning they would not have been able to go or come [back]; or, ﴿to proceed﴾ means [moving] forward before them;

﴿nor could they return﴾, meaning behind them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on Surah 36, verse 68:

﴿And whomever We grant long life, We reverse him in creation﴾. ʿĀṣim and Ḥamzah (read it as) *nunakkisuhu* (with *nūn* and the doubled *kāf*). *Al-tankīs* is making the top of a thing its bottom. The rest of the readers (read it as) *nankusuhu* (with *nūn* and an unmarked *kāf*).

﴿in creation﴾, that is: We turn him over in it. The meaning is: "Whoever We prolong the life of, We reverse his creation, so that in place of strength there is weakness, and in place of youth there is decrepitude. That is because We created him in weakness of body, devoid of intellect and knowledge. Then We made him increase until he reaches his full strength, completes his power, and comprehends and knows what is for him and what is against him. When he reaches that point, We reverse him in creation, making him diminish until he returns to a state resembling that of a child, in the weakness of his body, the scantiness of his intellect, and his lack of knowledge, just as an arrow is reversed so that its top becomes its bottom."

The Exalted and Majestic said: ﴿And among you is one who is returned to the most abject age, so that he knows nothing after having known﴾ [al-Ḥajj: 5]. ﴿Will they not then use their reason?﴾ (That is:) Will not the One who is able to move them from youth to old age, from strength to weakness, and from soundness of intellect to senility and lack of discernment, be able to obliterate their eyes, transform them in their places, and resurrect them after death?!

*Bi-l-tāʾ* (with the *tāʾ*, i.e., *tunakkisuhu*): Madani, Yaʿqub, and Sahl.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 36, verse 69:

They used to say to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "A poet." So it was revealed: ﴿And We did not teach him poetry﴾, meaning: We did not teach the Prophet (ﷺ) the speech of the poets. Or: "And We did not teach him poetry by teaching him the Qur'an," on the meaning that the Qur'an is not poetry. Rather, it is speech that is metrical and rhymed, yet conveys a meaning. Where is the meter? Where is the rhyme? There is no resemblance between it and poetry, if you examine it closely.

﴿And it is not befitting for him﴾: it is not right for him, nor suitable to his state, nor would it be sought from him even if he sought it. (p-111) That is: We made him such that if he had wanted to compose poetry, it would not have been possible for him nor easy, just as We made him unlettered, unable to be guided to writing, so that the proof would be more firmly established and the doubt more easily refuted. As for his saying (ﷺ): "I am the Prophet, there is no lie; I am the son of 'Abd al-Muttalib," and his saying: "Are you but a finger that bled, and in the way of Allah you have suffered what you have suffered," these are nothing but of the kind of his speech which he used to utter spontaneously, without craft in it or affectation, except that it happened, without intent to that and without his attention, that it came out metrical, just as there occur in people's sermons, letters and conversations things that are metrical, and no one calls them poetry, because their speaker did not intend meter. It is also the case that he (peace and blessings be upon him) said "laqīti" with a sukun, and he pronounced the "b" in "kadhiba" with a fatha and the "b" in "al-Muttalib" with a kasra.

When he negated that the Qur'an is of the kind of poetry, he said: ﴿It is not﴾, meaning: the one taught,

﴿but a reminder and a clear Qur'an﴾. That is: it is nothing but a reminder from Allah, by which mankind and jinn are admonished, and it is nothing but a Qur'an, a heavenly Book, which is read in the prayer niches, recited in acts of worship, and by its recitation and acting upon it one attains the success of both abodes. How far is it, then, from poetry, which is among the whisperings of the devils?!

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 36, verse 70:

﴿Liyundhira﴾ (that it may warn): the Qur'an, or the Messenger. [Read as] "Litundhira" (that you may warn) by Madani, Shami, Sahl and Ya'qub.

﴿man kana hayyan﴾ (whoever is living): one who is rational and reflective, because the heedless one is like the dead; or one who is alive in the heart.

﴿wa-yahiqqa al-qawl﴾ (and the word may be justified): and the word of punishment becomes binding (wajibah kalimat al-'adhab).

﴿'ala al-kafirin﴾ (against the disbelievers): those who do not reflect, and who are in the position of the dead.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 36, verse 71:

﴿Have they not seen that We have created for them, of what Our hands have done, livestock, so that they are their owners?﴾ That is: of what We Ourselves undertook to bring into existence, and which none other than Us was able to bring into existence.

﴿So they are its owners.﴾ That is: We created them for their sake, then made them possessors of them, so they dispose of them as owners do, and have exclusive benefit from them. Or: "So they are able to control them, and subdue them."

(p-112) ﴿And We have subjected them to them﴾, meaning, We made them submissive to them. Otherwise, who could control them were it not for His (Exalted be He) taming them and subjecting them to them? For this reason Allah, Glorified is He, obligated the rider to give thanks for this blessing and to glorify Him, by his saying: ﴿Glory be to Him who has subjected this to us, and we could not have subdued it ourselves﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 13]. ﴿So some of them they ride﴾, namely, that which is ridden,

﴿and of them they eat﴾, i.e., We subjected them to them so that they might ride their backs and eat their flesh.

Translation:

﴿And they have taken, besides Allah, gods, that perhaps they might be helped﴾. That is: perhaps their idols would help them when some matter afflicts them.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 36, verse 75:**

﴿They are not able﴾, that is, their gods, ﴿to help them﴾, the help of their worshippers,

﴿and they, for them﴾, that is, the disbelievers for the idols, ﴿are an army﴾, helpers and a faction, ﴿brought forward﴾, serving them and defending them. Or they took them so that they would help them before Allah and intercede for them. But the matter is contrary to what they imagined, since they, on the Day of Resurrection, are an army prepared for them, brought forward for their punishment, because they will be made fuel for the Fire.

﴿So let not their speech grieve you﴾. With the vowelling of the *ya'* (يَحْزُنْكَ read as *yaḥzunka*), and the *zay* kasra, Nafi' reads it as *yuḥzunka*, from *ḥazanahu* and *aḥzanahu*. The meaning is: "Let not their denial, their harm, and their harshness trouble you."

﴿Indeed We know what they conceal﴾, of their enmity,

﴿and what they reveal﴾. We will requite them for it. It is therefore fitting for one like you to take comfort in this warning and to call to mind, in his own soul, the image of his state and theirs in the Hereafter, until the worry lifts from him and grief does not overwhelm him. As for the one who claims that whoever reads *anna naʿlamu* (أنّا نَعْلَمُ) with a *fatḥa* has ruined his prayer, and that if he believes its meaning he has disbelieved, he is mistaken, because it can be taken as the omission of the *lam al-taʿlīl* (the lam of causation, meaning "because"). This omission is common in the Qur'an, in poetry, and in all speech. On this basis is the talbiyah of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "Verily (أنَّ) the praise and the blessing are Yours." Abu Hanifa read it with a *kasra*, and al-Shafi'i with a *fatḥa*, may God have mercy on them both, and both readings are causal.

If you say: if the *fatḥa* reading is a *badal* (substitution) for *qawluhum*, as though it were said, "So let not their speech grieve you, that We know what they conceal and what they reveal," then its corruption is evident. I say: this meaning also holds with the *kasra* if you make it the object of the verb of speech. It has become clear that the grief's connection to God's being knowing, and its absence of connection, do not turn on the *kasra* or *fatḥa* of *inna*, but on your reckoning. So you distinguish: if you read the *fatḥa*, you separate by assuming the meaning of causation and not assuming the meaning of substitution, just as you distinguish by assuming the meaning of causation when you read the *kasra* and not assuming the meaning of the object. Then, whether you read it with a *kasra* or a *fatḥa*, according to what that speaker found so grave, there is nothing in it but the prohibition of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ from grief, despite His (exalted be He) knowledge of their secret and their open speech. The prohibition against his grieving is not an affirmation of his grief over that, as in His saying: ﴿So never be a supporter of the disbelievers﴾ [al-Qasas: 86], meaning "and never be among the polytheists."

﴿And do not invoke with Allah any other deity﴾ [al-Qasas: 88]. It was revealed concerning Ubayy ibn Khalaf, when he took a decayed bone and began crumbling it in his hand, saying: "O Muhammad, do you think Allah will bring this back to life after it has crumbled to dust?" The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Yes, and He will resurrect you and cast you into Hell."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 36, verse 77:

﴿Has man not considered that We created him from a drop [of semen]﴾, a foul, emitted fluid, coming out of the urethra (al-ihlil), which is the passage of filth,

﴿and then he is an open adversary﴾, clearly contentious. That is: despite the humility of his origin and the baseness of his beginning, he sets himself up to dispute with his Lord and denies His power to bring the dead back to life after their bones have decayed. Then his disputing is about the most binding attribute of his and the one most closely attached to him, namely that he was created from something dead, and yet he denies that he was originated from something dead, which is the utmost obstinacy.

ÔWa-ḍaraba lanā mathalan (And he struck for Us a parable), by crushing the bone,

﴿وَنَسِيَ خَلْقَهُ﴾ — "and forgot his creation," that is, from the sperm-drop, so it is more strange than the revival of the bone. The verbal noun (al-maṣdar) is in the genitive construction (iḍāfa) with the object: that is, "Our creating him" (khalaqnā iyyāhu).

﴿قالَ مَن يُحْيِي العِظامَ وهي رَمِيمٌ﴾ — "He said: 'Who will give life to the bones when they are decayed?'" Ramīm is a noun (ism) for what has decayed of the bones, not an adjective (ghayr ṣifa), like "al-rumma" and "al-rufāt." For this reason it is not feminized, although it occurs as the predicate (khabar) of a feminine subject. Whoever affirms that there is life in the bones — and says that the bones of a dead person are impure, because death affects them, since life inheres in them — clings to this verse. But according to us they are pure, and likewise the hair and the sinews, because life does not inhere in them, so death has no effect on them. The meaning of "reviving the bones" in the verse is returning them to what they were, soft and moist, in a living, sensitive body.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 36, verse 79:

﴿Say: He will give them life who produced them the first time.﴾ "Produced" here means "created" (khalaqa).

﴿The first time﴾ means: at the beginning (ibtida'an).

﴿And He is, of every creation,﴾ every created thing (makhluq),

﴿Knowing.﴾ Nothing of it is hidden from Him, even if its parts are scattered over land and sea. He gathers them and returns them as they were.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 36, verse 80:

﴿Who has made for you fire from the green tree, and behold, from it you kindle.﴾ (taqdahun, "you strike forth [sparks]"). Then he mentioned, among the wonders of His creation, the striking forth of fire from the green tree, despite the opposition of fire to water and its being extinguished by it. This is the flint (al-zind, the means of kindling) with which the Bedouins (al-a'rab) produce fire. Most of it comes from al-markh (a kind of soft tree, Calotropis or similar) and al-'affar (another tree), and in their proverbs: "In every tree there is fire, and al-markh and al-'affar have become renowned." This is because al-markh is a tree that readily produces fire (al-wary, the kindling of fire), and al-'affar is a tree from which fire is struck. A man cuts from both of them two branches, like two siwak (toothsticks), and they are both green, with water dripping from them. He rubs al-markh, which is masculine, upon al-'affar, which is feminine, and fire is struck by the permission of Allah. And from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, he said: "There is no tree but that fire is in it, except al-'unnab (jujube), for the benefit of beating clothes with it." Whoever is able to gather water and fire in trees is able to alternate between death and life among mankind, and causing one of the two opposites to follow the other by succession is easier for the intellect than their joining together simultaneously without order. The word "al-akhdar" is read according to the wording (al-lafz), and it was read "al-khadra'" according to the meaning (al-ma'na). Then he explained that whoever is able to create the heavens and the earth, despite their greatness, is more capable of creating humans, by His saying:

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 36, verse 81:

﴿Is not He who created the heavens and the earth able to create the like of them?﴾ — in smallness, relative to the heavens and the earth — or to restore them, because the return (al-ma'ad) is like the initial origination (al-mubtada'), and it is not unlike it. (p-115)

﴿Yes indeed﴾, i.e., say: "Yes indeed, He is capable of that."

﴿And He is the All-Creating (al-Khallaq)﴾, the One who has many creations.

﴿The All-Knowing (al-'Alim)﴾, the One who has many things known.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 36, verse 82:

﴿Indeed, His command﴾: His matter, His affair,

﴿when He intends a thing, is that He says to it, "Be,"﴾: that He bring it into existence,

﴿and it is.﴾ That is, it comes into being. "So it is existent and present, without doubt." The upshot is that all created things come to be through His creating and bringing them into being. However, He expressed His bringing-into-being with the word "Be" (kun), though there was no kaf or nun involved. This is rather an illustration of the speed of bringing into being, as if He were saying: "Just as the word 'Be' is not burdensome for you, so too the origination of creation and their return is not burdensome for Allah." The reading "fa-yakūnu" (and it is) with the damma on the nun is that of Ibn Amir (Shami) and Ali (Ali), where it is conjoined to "yaqūla" (He says). As for the raf' (nominative vowel), it is because it is a nominal sentence consisting of a subject and predicate, its implied form being "fa-huwa yakūnu" (so He is bringing it into being), conjoined to a similar sentence, namely "His command is that He says to it, 'Be.'"

﴿Subhan﴾ (Glory be to Him): a declaration that He is exempt from what the polytheists attribute to Him, and an expression of wonder that they should say what they say about Him.

﴿Alladhi biyadihi malakut kulli shay'in﴾ (He in whose hand is the dominion of everything). That is, the sovereignty (mulk) of everything. The addition of the waw and the taa' in *malakut* is for emphasis, meaning: He is the owner of everything.

﴿Wa ilayhi turja'un﴾ (And to Him you will be returned): you will be brought back after death, without any escape. The verb "turja'un" is read by Ya'qub (Ya'qub al-Hadrami, one of the recognised Qur'an readers) as "turja'un" with the vowels reversed, so that it reads "tarji'un". [Note: the commentary's text reads "تَرْجِعُونَ" and "تُرْجَعُونَ"; the reading difference is between the active and passive forms of the verb.]

The Messenger of God (peace be upon him) said: "Every thing has a heart, and the heart of the Qur'an is Ya-Sin. Whoever recites Ya-Sin, seeking thereby the face of God, God will forgive him, and he will be given a reward as if he had recited the Qur'an twenty-two times."

He (peace be upon him) also said: "Whoever recites Ya-Sin before his need, his need will be fulfilled for him."

He (peace be upon him) also said: "Whoever recites it while hungry, God will satisfy him; if he is thirsty, God will quench him; if he is naked, God will clothe him; if he is afraid, God will give him security; if he is lonely, God will give him companionship; if he is poor, God will make him rich; if he is in prison, God will bring him out; if he is a captive, God will free him; if he is astray, God will guide him; if he is in debt, God will pay his debt from His treasuries."

It is called "al-Dafi'a" (the Repeller) and "al-Qadiya" (the Fulfiller of needs), for it repels every evil from its reciter and fulfils for him every need.
